adj:frei.tx: From Middle High German vrî, Old High German frî, from Proto-West Germanic *frī. Compare Dutch vrij, English free, Danish fri.

adj:feist.tx: From Middle High German veizet, from Old High German feizzit, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid, whence also the doublet fett (through Middle Low German).

verb:fallen.tx: From Middle High German vallen, from Old High German fallan, from Proto-West Germanic *fallan, from Proto-Germanic *fallaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pōl-. Akin to Bavarian foin, Low German fallen, Dutch vallen, English fall, Danish falde, Dutch falla.

num:fünf.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vünf, from Old High German fimf, from Proto-West Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. Formal cognates include Dutch vijf, English five, Yiddish פֿינף (finf), Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌼𐍆 (fimf) and Icelandic fimm.

adj:französisch.tx: From Middle High German franzoisisch, franzoisch (franzois, franzoys, franzeis), borrowed from Old French françois + -isch. Analysable as Franzose (“Frenchman”) + -isch. Replaced Middle High German franzisch, from francisc, frenkisc, Old High German frenkisk.

adv:fast.tx: From Middle High German vast, vaste, from Old High German fasto (“solidly, strictly, securely”), from Proto-West Germanic *fastō, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz. Cognate with Middle Low German vaste (whence German Low German fast), English fast (adverb). Compare also German fest, English fast (adjective), Dutch vast.

noun:Fisch.tx: From Middle High German visch, from Old High German fisk, fisc, from Proto-West Germanic *fisk.

noun:Feder.tx: From Middle High German vëdere, from Old High German fëdara (akin to Old Saxon fethara), from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”). Compare Low German Fedder, Dutch veder, veer, English feather, Danish fjer, Swedish fjäder.

noun:Fenster.tx: From Middle High German vënster, from Old High German fënstar, from Proto-West Germanic *fenestr (“window”).

noun:Flusspferd.tx: From Fluss (“river”) + Pferd (“horse”). Calque of Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos).

adj:fair.tx: Borrowed from English fair in the 19th century, from Old English fæġer, from Proto-West Germanic *fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz, whence also Middle High German vager (“splendid, wonderful”).

noun:Fernweh.tx: From fern (“far”) + Weh (“pain”), literally “far pain” or “far sickness”, as contrasted with Heimweh (“homesickness, longing for home”).

noun:Fahrrad.tx: From fahren (“drive/ride”) + Rad (“wheel”). Compare Dutch rijwiel.

noun:Freude.tx: From Middle High German vröude, from Old High German frewida, from Proto-Germanic *frawiþō (“joy”), derived from *frawaz (“joyous”), from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“to jump; hop”). Cognate with Dutch vreugde, Low German Freid, Danish fryd, Swedish fröjd.

adj:final.tx: 18th century, from Latin finālis, perhaps in part through French final. Recently revived to some degree by influence of English final.

noun:Fuchs.tx: From Middle High German vuhs, from Old High German fuhs, from Proto-West Germanic *fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *púḱsos (“the tailed one”), from *puḱ- (“tail”). Cognate with English fox, Sanskrit पुच्छ (púccha).

adj:fame.tx: Probably a clipped borrowing from English famous, likely influenced by the similarly borrowed Fame which serves as its noun equivalent. Attested by the mid-2000s.

verb:fangen.tx: From Middle High German vāhen, from Old High German fāhan, a strong verb with past forms fieng, gefangan, from Proto-West Germanic *fą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną. The present stem fang- is derived from the past forms. This development spread from Middle Low German vangen to Central German dialects of early modern German (compare already Old Saxon fangan alongside fāhan). The same happened …

adj:fix.tx: Inherited from Middle High German fix, influenced by French fixe.

adj:frank.tx: From Middle High German franc, from Old French franc (“free”), of Germanic but eventually uncertain origin.

adj:fade.tx: Borrowed from French fade, from Vulgar Latin fatidus.

adj:fancy.tx: Borrowed from English fancy. Doublet of Fantasie.

noun:Farbe.tx: From Middle High German varwe, from Old High German farawa, from Proto-West Germanic *faru, from Proto-Germanic *farwō.

verb:fahren.tx: From Middle High German varn, varen, from Old High German faran, from Proto-West Germanic *faran. Cognate with Dutch varen, English fare, Danish fare.

adj:fatal.tx: 17th century, from Latin fātālis, in part through French fatal.

adj:fest.tx: From Middle High German vest, from Old High German festi, from Proto-West Germanic *fast, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz; see there for cognates and further etymology.

adj:fundamental.tx: Borrowed from Latin fundāmentālis. By surface analysis, Fundament + -al.

noun:Frau.tx: From Middle High German vrouwe, from Old High German frouwa (“mistress”), from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjā, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ, a feminine form of *frawjô (“lord”), giving Old English frēa (“lord, king; God, Christ; husband”), frēo (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *proHwo-, a derivation from *per- (“to go forward”). Cognate with Old Saxon frūa (hence Middle Low German vrouwe, Modern …

noun:Feuer.tx: From Middle High German viur, from Old High German fiur, from Proto-West Germanic *fuir. Cognate with Dutch vuur, Low German Füer, West Frisian fjoer, English fire, Danish fyr.

adj:frugal.tx: Borrowed from French frugal, from Latin frugalis.

verb:ficken.tx: From Middle High German ficken (“to rub, solidify, strengthen”), perhaps from Old High German *fuchōn, *fuhhōn (attested in fitafuchōn, fitafuhhōn (“to yearn for, seek or solicit fornication”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“to stick, sting, stab”). The interjectional use is probably a semantic loan from English fuck. Alternatively, perhaps related to Middle Low German vicken, …

intj:ficken.tx: From Middle High German ficken (“to rub, solidify, strengthen”), perhaps from Old High German *fuchōn, *fuhhōn (attested in fitafuchōn, fitafuhhōn (“to yearn for, seek or solicit fornication”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“to stick, sting, stab”). The interjectional use is probably a semantic loan from English fuck. Alternatively, perhaps related to Middle Low German vicken, …

adj:fern.tx: From Middle High German vërren, from Old High German fërrana, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ferrai, same as English far.

prep:fern.tx: From Middle High German vërren, from Old High German fërrana, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ferrai, same as English far.

noun:Ferkel.tx: From Middle High German verkelen, byform of verhelīn, from Old High German farhilī, farhilīn, diminutive of farah (“pig”), from Proto-West Germanic *farh, from Proto-Germanic *farhaz (whence English farrow), from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos. The -k- has been explained as an irregular fortition of -h-, which would be plausible if the form were of Upper German origin, where -h- was strong and where …

noun:Frischling.tx: From Middle High German vrischinc, Old High German frisking (“beast of offering”).

verb:fasten.tx: Middle High German vasten, from Old High German fastēn, from Proto-West Germanic *fastēn.

adv:fort.tx: From Middle High German vort, Old High German forth, Proto-West Germanic *forþ, compare English forth, Dutch voort.

noun:Fahrenheit.tx: Named after Prussian scientist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit. The surname is poorly attested and of uncertain origin, but superficially composed of fahren (“to go, travel”) + the suffix -heit.

conj:falls.tx: Presumably from the genitive of Fall.

noun:Führer.tx: From Middle High German füerære, vüerære, füerer, vüerer, from Old High German fôrari, equivalent to führen (“to lead”) + -er. Cognate with Yiddish פֿירער (firer), Cimbrian büurar, Swedish förare. In the historical sense probably a calque of Italian Duce.

noun:Frucht.tx: From Middle High German fruht, vruht, from Old High German fruht, from Proto-West Germanic *fruhti (“fruit”). Cognate with Alemannic German Frucht, Hunsrik Frucht.

noun:Fuß.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vuoȥ, from Old High German fuoȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts (“foot”) (compare West Frisian foet, Dutch voet, Low German Foot, English foot, Danish fod), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

num:fünfzig.tx: From Middle High German vünfzic, from Old High German fimfzug, from Proto-Germanic *fimf tigiwiz. Equivalent to fünf + -zig.

noun:Fleisch.tx: From Middle High German fleisch, vleisch, from Old High German fleisk, from Proto-West Germanic *flaiski.

noun:Flasche.tx: From Middle High German flasche, from Old High German flasca (“bottle”), from Proto-West Germanic *flaskā, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”), from *flehtaną (“to plait, braid”), from the practice of plaiting or wrapping bottles in straw casing. Cognate to English flask. Doublet of Fiasko and Flakon.

noun:Freitag.tx: From Middle High German vrītac, from Old High German frīatag (9th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag (“day of Frigg”), calque of Latin dies Veneris. Compare Low German Freedag, Dutch vrijdag, English Friday, Danish fredag.

adj:fossil.tx: From Latin fossilis (“something which has been dug up”), from fodio (“to dig up”).

noun:Flut.tx: From Middle High German vluot, Old High German fluot, from Proto-West Germanic *flōdu, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz. Compare Dutch vloed, English flood, Danish flod, Icelandic flóð.

noun:Freund.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vriunt, from Old High German friunt, from Proto-West Germanic *friund, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (“lit., the loving one; lover, loved one, friend”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *preyH-. Cognate with Dutch vriend, German Low German Fründ, Luxembourgish Frënd, West Frisian freon, English friend, Danish frænde (“relative”), Faroese frændi (“friend, …

noun:Fahrzeug.tx: Compound of fahren (“travel”) + Zeug (“equipment”), which is a calque of Middle Low German vārtüch. The word was originally restricted to vessels, as still is Dutch vaartuig.

noun:Fall.tx: From Middle High German val, from Old High German fal, from Proto-West Germanic *fall. Cognate with Dutch val, English fall. The sense “case” in all its shapes is a calque of Latin casus.

noun:Falter.tx: Haplology of dialectal German Feifalter, from Middle High German vīvalter, from Old High German fīfaltra, from Proto-Germanic *fifaldǭ, *fīfildǭ (“butterfly”), from Proto-Indo-European *peypel-. Cognate with Dutch vijfwouter, Icelandic fiðrildi, and outside Germanic Latin papilio. Folk-etymologically re-interpreted as Zweifalter, Pfeiffalter, etc., by association with unrelated falten (“to fold”).

noun:Fan.tx: Borrowed from English fan, short for fanatic.

noun:Fang.tx: From Middle High German vanc, ultimately from the root of fangen (“to catch”).

noun:Farm.tx: 19th century, from English farm, which see. The feminine gender may have been influenced by related French ferme f and/or by the synonym Zucht f.

noun:Farmer.tx: Either directly borrowed from English farmer or formed in German as Farm + -er.

noun:Fasten.tx: Plural of the synonymous (obsolete) Faste, from Middle High German vaste, from Old High German fasta. See the verb fasten.

noun:Faust.tx: From Middle High German fūst, vūst, voust, from Old High German fūst.

noun:Fee.tx: Middle High German fei(n)e. Borrowed from French fée, from Latin fata.

noun:Fell.tx: From Middle High German vël, from Old High German fël, from Proto-West Germanic *fell.

noun:Fellatio.tx: From Latin fēllātiō. In the late 19th century still treated as a Latin word; see quotation using italics and lower case for a noun.

noun:Fermium.tx: Borrowed from New Latin fermium, named after atomic physicist Enrico Fermi. For the surname see Fermi.

noun:Fest.tx: From Middle High German fëst, derived from Latin festum. Cognate with English feast, French fête, Italian festa.

noun:Filter.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin filtrum under the influence of the verb filtern, borrowed earlier from the same source. Additional senses beyond the physical one are typically semantic borrowings from English.

noun:Finale.tx: Borrowed from Italian finale in the 17th c., initially in the form Final. Pfeifer also considers a direct borrowing from Latin fīnālis on account of the Italian term potentially being attested later. The sports sense is a 20th c. semantic loan from English final.

noun:Finger.tx: From Middle High German vinger, Old High German fingar, from Proto-West Germanic *fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz, from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷrós. Compare Low German Finger, Dutch vinger, English finger, Danish finger, Yiddish פֿינגער (finger).

noun:Firma.tx: Borrowed from Italian firma. Cognate with English firm.

noun:First.tx: From Middle High German virst, from Old High German first, perhaps ultimately from a combination of Proto-Indo-European *per- + *steh₂-, similar to Proto-Indo-Iranian *pr̥štʰás (“ridge, back”), Latin postis (“doorpost”), Ancient Greek παστάς (pastás, “porch”).

noun:Flame.tx: Compare Middle High German Flemming; Flæminge (plural), Dutch Vlaming, English Fleming.

noun:Flamme.tx: From Middle High German vlamme, from Old High German flamma (10th c.), from Latin flamma.

noun:Fleck.tx: From Middle High German vlëc, from Old High German flëk, from Proto-West Germanic *flekkō, from Proto-Germanic *flekka- (“spot, mark”). Cognate with Dutch vlek, English fleck.

noun:Fleet.tx: From German Low German and Middle Low German vlēt, from Old Saxon fliot, from Proto-West Germanic *fleut, from Proto-Germanic *fleutą (“stream, river”). Cognate to Dutch vliet, English fleet.

noun:Flipper.tx: From English flipper (“lever in a pinball machine used to strike the ball”). The senses "pinball" and "pinball machine" are a pseudo-anglicism, with "flipper" being used in many languages to refer the game of pinball; see flipper.

noun:Flor.tx: Borrowed from Dutch floers, a borrowing from French velours. Doublet of Velours.

noun:Fluid.tx: Borrowed from English fluid borrowed from Latin fluidus.

noun:Fluke.tx: Probably from English fluke, which see. Appears not to be attested before the 19th century.

noun:Form.tx: From Middle High German form, from Latin forma.

noun:Fossil.tx: Borrowed from French fossile, from Latin fossilis (“unearthed, dug up”).

noun:Fotze.tx: From Middle High German fotze, votze, futze, probably from Proto-Germanic *fuþiz (“vagina”). Duden instead derives it from the same source of faul (“foul, something stinky”). See also Middle High German fut, vut (“sheath, vagina, vulva”), German Fut. Akin to Bavarian Fotzen (“a slap in the face, on the mouth and the mouth itself”), Dutch vot (“arse”), Hunsrik Futz (“cunt”), Kölsch Fott …

noun:Foul.tx: Borrowed from English foul. Doublet of faul.

noun:Fragment.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin fragmentum.

noun:Frost.tx: From Middle High German vrost, from Old High German frost, from Proto-West Germanic *frost, from Proto-Germanic *frustaz. Cognate with Dutch vorst, English frost, Icelandic frost.

noun:Fund.tx: From Middle High German vunt (“finding, discovery, find”), ultimately from the root of finden. Cognate with Old Norse fundr, Dutch vond (“discovery, invention”).

noun:Funk.tx: Back-formation from funken, Funker, themselves from Funkentelegraphie, from Funken (“spark”) + Telegraphie (“telegraphy”).

noun:Frankfurter.tx: From Frankfurt + -er. (sausage): Gender from Frankfurter Wurst f

verb:fensterln.tx: From the South German dialectal diminutive Fensterl (“small window”), from Fenster.

noun:Flucht.tx: From Middle High German vluht, from Old High German fluht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti (“escape”). Pertaining to fliehen (“to flee”).

verb:fliehen.tx: From Middle High German vliehen, from Old High German fliohan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleuhan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuhaną. Cognate with Dutch vlieden and English flee.

noun:Ferse.tx: Old High German fersana, from Proto-Germanic *fersnō (“heel”).

noun:Färse.tx: From Late Middle High German verse, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *farsijā, derived (with Verner alternation) from Proto-Germanic *farzaz (“bull, ox”), whence obsolete German Farre. Cognate with Dutch vaars. The word is not attested in High German before the 15th century and apparently alien to modern dialects outside the borderlands with Low German. Therefore likely borrowed through Middle …

noun:Fritzchen.tx: Diminutive Form of Fritz, which is short for Friedrich. Cognate to Freddy.

noun:Frikadelle.tx: Late 17th century, borrowed from Dutch frikadel (attested 1607), itself from French fricadel(le). The French is only recorded in 1742, but its earlier existence is likely as it is a variant of fricandeau (1548), which see. A further relation with Italian frittatella is speculative. Derivation of German Frikadelle from Italian instead of Dutch (as suggested in some sources) is implausible in view …

adj:frivol.tx: Borrowed from French frivole, from Latin frīvolus.

noun:Fett.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German vette; see fett for more.

adj:fett.tx: From Middle Low German vet, from Old Saxon *fētid, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid. Doublet of feist. In the colloquial sense perhaps a calque of English phat via hip-hop culture.

verb:fliegen.tx: From Middle High German vliegen, Old High German fliogan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleugan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-. Compare Bavarian fliagn, Dutch vliegen, Low German flegen, English fly, Danish flyve.

verb:finden.tx: From Middle High German vinden, from Old High German findan, from Proto-West Germanic *finþan, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną. Cognate with Bavarian findn, Alemannic German finde, Low German finden, Dutch vinden, English find, Danish finde.

verb:fragen.tx: From Middle High German vrāgen, from Old High German frāgēn, frahēn/frāhēn, which is indirectly derived from Proto-West Germanic *frāgēn. Cognate with Alemannic German frage (“to ask”), Saterland Frisian fräigje (“to ask”), Dutch vragen (“to ask”), Low German fragen (“to ask”), English frain (“to ask, inquire”), Swedish fråga (“to ask”), Icelandic fregna (“to hear of, learn about”).

noun:Fernsehen.tx: From fern + sehen (“far-see”), a calque of French télévision.

verb:fernsehen.tx: Compound of fern + sehen, derived from the noun Fernsehen.

noun:Frosch.tx: From Middle High German vrosch, from Old High German frosk (“frog”), from Proto-West Germanic *frosk (“frog”), from Proto-Germanic *fruskaz (“frog”), from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“jump, hop”). Cognate with Middle Low German vorsch (“frog”), Dutch vors, West Frisian froask, Icelandic froskur, dialectal English frosh (“frog”).

noun:Falle.tx: From Middle High German valle, Old High German falla, deverbal from fallen. Compare typologically Czech past, Polish zapadnia, Russian западня́ (zapadnjá) (akin to па́дать (pádatʹ), па́сть (pástʹ)).

verb:fällen.tx: From Middle High German vellen, Old High German fellen, from Proto-West Germanic *fallijan, from Proto-Germanic *fallijaną (“to make fall”), causative of *fallaną. Cognate with English fell.

verb:füttern.tx: From Middle High German vüetern, from Old High German fuotiren, derived from fuotar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder”). Equivalent to Futter + -n. Compare Dutch voeren (“to feed”), dialectal English to fodder.

verb:fressen.tx: From Middle High German vrëȥȥen, from Old High German frëȥȥan, firëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraetan. Cognate with Dutch vreten, English fret, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (fraitan), Swedish fräta.

noun:Filzlaus.tx: 15th century, from Filz (“felt”, also “tangled, clotted hair”) + Laus (“louse”).

noun:Filz.tx: From Middle High German vilz, from Old High German filz, from Proto-West Germanic *felt, akin to Old Saxon filt. More at English felt.

noun:Fahne.tx: From Middle High German van(e) m, from Old High German fano, from Proto-West Germanic *fanō, from Proto-Germanic *fanô (“cloth, flag”), from Proto-Indo-European *pān- (“fabric”). The shift to the feminine gender began in cognate Middle Low German vāne and, through Central German, established itself in the written language by the end of the 17th century.

verb:folgen.tx: From Middle High German volgen, from Old High German folgēn, from Proto-West Germanic *folgēn, from Proto-Germanic *fulgāną. Doublet of followen.

noun:Fassade.tx: Borrowed from French façade, ultimately from Latin faciēs (“face”).

noun:Forelle.tx: With irregular stress shift (as in Holunder, lebendig, etc.) from Middle High German forhel, alteration of older forhen, from Old High German forhana, from Proto-Germanic *furhnō, from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- (“speckled”).

verb:funktionieren.tx: Ca. 1800, from Funktion + -ieren, likely after French fonctionner.

noun:Fels.tx: From Middle High German vels, from Old High German felis, from Proto-West Germanic *falis, from Proto-Germanic *falisaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pels-, *pelis- (“rock, cliff”). Compare Old Norse fjall (“rock, mountain”), Ancient Greek πέλλα (pélla, “stone”), Old Irish ail (“cliff”). The variant Felsen emerged from the oblique cases.

noun:Fliege.tx: From Middle High German fliege, vliege, from Old High German flioga, from Proto-Germanic *fleugǭ. Cognate with Old English flēoġe (>English fly).

adj:finster.tx: From Middle High German vinster, from Old High German finstar.

noun:Feld.tx: From Middle High German vëlt, from Old High German fëld, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, from Proto-Germanic *felþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂-. Cognates include Dutch veld and English field.

noun:Frechdachs.tx: From frech (“insulting, barefaced, naughty, rude”) + Dachs (“badger”).

adj:frech.tx: From Middle High German vrëch, from Old High German frëh, from Proto-West Germanic *frek. Cognate with Dutch vrek, Icelandic frekur. Compare also English freak.

num:fünfzehn.tx: From Middle High German vünfzehen, from Old High German fimfzehan, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun. Equivalent to fünf + zehn. Compare Dutch vijftien, West Frisian fyftjin, English fifteen, Danish femten, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌼𐍆𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌿𐌽 (fimftaihun).

noun:Fichte.tx: From Middle High German viehte, Old High German fiuhta, from Proto-West Germanic *fiuhtijā.

noun:Flug.tx: From Middle High German vluc, from Old High German flug, from Proto-Germanic *flugiz.

noun:Flughafen.tx: From Flug (“flight”) + Hafen (“port”). Compare Icelandic flughöfn.

noun:Fass.tx: From Middle High German vaz, from Old High German faȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *fat. Cognate with Dutch vat, English vat, fat (which see).

noun:Fidschi.tx: Ultimately from Fijian Viti Levu (“Great Viti”).

noun:Flanke.tx: Ca. 1600, from French flanc, from Old French flanc, from Proto-West Germanic *hlanku. Doublet of now obsolete Lanke, which likely influenced the form and gender of the borrowing; analogy with Seite may also have contributed.

adj:fahl.tx: From Middle High German val (inflected valwe), from Old High German falo, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz. While the variant falb is from the Middle High German inflected stem, the form fahl is based on the uninflected stem. However, the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce -lw- to -l- even in open syllables; these include Middle Low German vāl (declined vāle), from Old Saxon …

noun:Fluss.tx: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Old High German fluȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *fluti, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, ultimately from the same root of fließen (“to flow”). Not cognate with Latin fluvius, which derives instead from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlewH-.

noun:Flügel.tx: From Middle High German vlügel, from Old High German *flugil, from Proto-Germanic *flugilaz. Cognate with Yiddish פֿליגל (fligl), Dutch vleugel, Middle Low German vlȫgel. The use for the grand piano (18th c.) is due to the similarity in form to a bird’s wing.

adj:flink.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German flink (“gleaming”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”).

noun:Fischstäbchen.tx: Compound of Fisch + Stäbchen. Compare Polish paluszek rybny.

noun:Fischer.tx: From Middle High German vischære, vischer, from Old High German fiscari, from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz.

noun:Flunder.tx: 15th century (East Prussian), also vluder, from Middle Low German vlundere, from Old Saxon *flunthria, eventually from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. The High German word must be from Low German given the marine context. However, Low German attestations are equally late and there are some indications that the word was not originally widely known. It may have been regionally restricted, or otherwise a …

noun:Fledermaus.tx: From Middle High German vledermūs, from Old High German fledarmūs, from *fledara (“wing”) + mūs (“mouse”). Displaced older mūstro (“bat”), found also in the combination form fledaremūstro/fledarmūstro.

noun:Flöte.tx: From Middle High German vloite and variants; borrowed via Middle Dutch floite from Old French fleüte.

noun:Flosse.tx: From Middle High German vlozze, from Old High German flozza, from Proto-Germanic *flutô. More at float.

noun:Fußball.tx: From Fuß (“foot”) + Ball (“ball”), a calque of English football. Doublet of the later borrowing Football (“American football”).
