noun:Frühstück.tx: From Middle High German vrüestücke (14th c.). Equivalent to früh (“early”) + Stück (“piece”, here in the sense of “bite”).

verb:fischen.tx: From Middle High German vischen, from Old High German fiskon, from Proto-West Germanic *fiskōn. By surface analysis, Fisch + -en.

adj:fulminant.tx: From Latin fulmināns (“striking with lightning”) via French fulminant.

prep:für.tx: From Middle High German vür, from Old High German furi, from Proto-West Germanic *furi, from Proto-Germanic *furi. Historically also used interchangeably with the related vor in its locational sense. In the 18th century, grammarians established a clearer split with für being prescribed for its chief modern senses of "for (the benefit of), in exchange for".

adj:falsch.tx: From Middle High German valsche, valsch, from Old High German *falski, from Proto-West Germanic *falskī (“false, counterfeit”).

noun:Freiheit.tx: From Middle High German vrīheit, from Old High German frīheit. Equivalent to frei (“free”) + heit (“-hood”). Compare Silesian Freiheet, Paderbornisch Low German Fryheit, Dutch vrijheid

noun:Fritz.tx: Shortened form of Friedrich. Cognate to English Fred.

noun:Frieden.tx: From Middle High German vride, from Old High German fridu. See also Dutch vrede, Danish fred, Swedish fred, English frith (“peace”). Starting in the 18th century, the weak form Friede started shifting to strong Frieden through spread of the ending from the oblique forms.

noun:Frevel.tx: From Middle High German vrevel, Old High German fravili, Proto-West Germanic *frafal(i).

noun:Fronleichnam.tx: From Middle High German vrōnlīcham, from Old High German vrōn (genitive singular of vrō (“lord”), from Proto-Germanic *frawjô) + līhhamo (“body”) (from *līkahamô).

verb:fügen.tx: From Middle High German füegen, fuogen, from Old High German fuogen, from Proto-West Germanic *fōgijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to join, attach”). Cognate with Dutch voegen and dated English fay, which is related to English fair. Also distantly related to English peace and pact through Latin.

noun:Fleiß.tx: From Middle High German flīȥ, vlīȥ, from Old High German flīȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *flītan (“to strive”), from Proto-Germanic *flītaz, *flītiz (“strife, zeal, effort, diligence”). Cognate with German Low German Fliet, Dutch vlijt, Saterland Frisian Fliet, English flite.

noun:Floß.tx: From Middle High German vlōz n, m, from Old High German flōz n, ultimately from the root of fließen (“to flow”). Compare Dutch vlot (“raft”), a related but different formation.

noun:Fessel.tx: From Middle High German veȥȥel, Old High German feȥȥil (“band for fastening and holding the sword”), from Proto-Germanic *fatilaz, from the root of *fatōną (“to hold, seize”). Cognate with Old Norse fetill (“band, bandage, sword-belt”), Old English fetel (“sword-belt”).

verb:fassen.tx: From Middle High German vaȥȥen, from Old High German faȥȥōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną (“to fetch, hold”). Cognate with English fetch.

verb:fließen.tx: From Middle High German vlieȥen, from Old High German flioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleutan, from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną, akin to English fleet (verb), Old Saxon fliotan and Dutch vlieten.

verb:falten.tx: From Middle High German valden, valten, from Old High German faldan, faltan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan. The irregular forms with -t- arose through early levelling of Grammatischer Wechsel, but remained rare in both Old and Middle High German. They probably established themselves in modern German by analogy as there are several verbs in -alten (halten, schalten, spalten, walten), but none in -alden.

adj:feucht.tx: From Middle High German viuchte, from Old High German fūht, from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *funhtijaz (“humid, wet, damp”). Cognate with the Dutch noun vocht (“liquid; dampness”).

verb:fürchten.tx: From Middle High German vürhten, from Old High German furihtan. Synchronically analyzed as Furcht + -en.

noun:Fuhre.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vuore (“journey; fodder”), from Old High German fuora, from Proto-West Germanic *fōru, from Proto-Germanic *fōrō (“a going; a traveling; a journey”), from *faraną (“to go; to travel”), from Proto-Indo-European *per-. Cognate with Old English fōr (“journey”), Luxembourgish Fouer, Vilamovian für, Yiddish פֿור (fur), Plautdietsch Fua.

noun:Floh.tx: From Middle High German vlō(ch), from Old High German flōh, from Proto-West Germanic *flauh. Cognate with Dutch vlo, English flea, Icelandic fló.

adj:fünfte.tx: From Old High German fimfto, from Proto-Germanic *fimftô. Equivalent to fünf + -te. Cognate with English fifth, Dutch vijfde, Old Saxon fīfto.

noun:Fohlen.tx: From Middle High German vole, fole, from Old High German folo, from Proto-West Germanic *folō, from Proto-Germanic *fulô. Old High German fulīn (whence modern Füllen) is originally a diminutive of the same root. The development by which the two words were perceived as mere phonetic variants started in Middle Low German volen vs. völlen. Thereby the word became neuter and took the nominative …

noun:Friseur.tx: Possibly from rare French friseur, first attested 1551. Alternatively an independent pseudo-French formation from frisieren + -eur. Most northern and eastern European languages that have this word probably borrowed it from German. Compare Polish fryzjer, Danish frisør, etc.

noun:Feuerwerk.tx: From Middle High German viurwerc (“fuel, firewood”, 14th c.). By surface analysis, Feuer (“fire”) + Werk (“works, implement”). In the modern sense since the 16th century. Compare Dutch vuurwerk, English fireworks.

noun:Fehler.tx: From fehlen in the sense of “to fail”.

verb:fehlen.tx: From Middle High German vælen, velen, valen, from Old French falir, faillir, from Latin fallō. Cognate with English fail.

noun:Flieder.tx: Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German vlêder, vlider (“elder”), itself probably from Middle Dutch vlieder, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fleuþr. Cognate with modern Dutch vlier, West Frisian flear. At first merely a northern synonym of Holunder (“elder”); then in the 18th century transferred to the somewhat similar-looking lilac, which is of southeastern European origin and thus had no German name.

noun:Föhre.tx: From Middle High German vorhe, from Old High German forha, from Proto-West Germanic *furhu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *furhō. While the word is now used especially in the south, the form with loss of post-liquid -h- is originally chiefly Central German; compare the variant above. Cognate with English fir.

noun:Fracht.tx: From Middle Low German vracht, alongside vrecht. The form with -a- (see also Dutch vracht) may ultimately be from Old Frisian.

noun:Futter.tx: From Middle High German vuoter, from Old High German fuotar (“fodder”). Compare Dutch voer, voeder, English fodder, Danish foder.

noun:Falz.tx: Middle High German valz, from the root of falzen (“to fold”).

verb:falzen.tx: From Middle High German valzen, velzen, from Old High German falzjan, gafalzjan, ultimately from the root of falten (“to fold”).

noun:Fahrt.tx: From Old High German vart, from Proto-West Germanic *fardi, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz, derived from *faraną (“to go, travel”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“going, passage”). Cognate with Dutch vaart, Swedish färd, English fard, ferd. Equivalent to a deverbal from fahren.

noun:Fabel.tx: From Middle High German fabele, from Old French fable, from Latin fabula.

noun:Fach.tx: From Middle High German vach, from Old High German fah, from Proto-West Germanic *fak, from Proto-Germanic *faką.

noun:Fächer.tx: 15th century, from fachen (“to stoke, stir up fire”) + -er. The verb is derived from Latin focō. The noun might also be a direct borrowing from Latin focārius (“he who stokes the hearth fire”), but this is unlikely.

noun:Fackel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vackel, from Old High German faccala, fackala, fackila, fackula, fackla, from Proto-West Germanic *fakkulā (“torch”).

noun:Faden.tx: From Middle High German vadem, from Old High German fadum, from Proto-West Germanic *faþm (“embrace”).

noun:Fähre.tx: From northern Middle High German ver(e) (13th c.), from Old High German *fera, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ (“ferry”), derived from *farjaną (“to bring, carry”), the causative of *faraną (“to travel”), whence German fahren. Analogy with this verb caused the modern ⟨ä⟩-spelling. The word was at first chiefly Central German, later being reinforced by cognate Middle Low German vēre. Upper German …

noun:Falke.tx: From Middle High German valke, from Old High German falco, from Proto-West Germanic *falkō, from Proto-Germanic *falkô.

noun:Falte.tx: From Middle High German valt, from Old High German falt. Related to the verb falten (“to fold”)

noun:Farn.tx: From Middle High German varn, from Old High German farn, from Proto-West Germanic *farn, from Proto-Indo-European *pornóm (“feather, wing; fern, leaf”), from *p(t)erH- (“fern”). Cognate with English fern, West Frisian fear, Dutch varen, Lithuanian spar̃nas, Avestan 𐬞𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬀 (par^əna), Kamkata-viri por, Sanskrit पर्ण (parṇá).

noun:Faser.tx: From Late Middle High German vaser, variant of vase, from Old High German fasa, faso (“fibre”). Cognate with Dutch vezel, Middle Low German vēse, Old English fæs.

noun:Feier.tx: From Middle High German vîre, from Old High German fîra, from Latin fēriae.

noun:Ferien.tx: 15th century, from Latin fēriae, with replacement of the Latin plural suffix -ae with German -en.

noun:Feige.tx: From Middle High German vīge, from Old High German fīga, from Proto-West Germanic *fīgā (“fig”).

noun:Feile.tx: From Middle High German fīle, fīhel, from Old High German fīla, fī(h)ila, fīhala, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō.

noun:Feind.tx: From Middle High German vīant, from Old High German fīant, fīand, from Proto-West Germanic *fijand, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz. Cognate to Low German Feend, Fiend, Icelandic fjandi, Dutch vijand, English fiend, Danish fjende, Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌾𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍃 (fijands), Yiddish פֿײַנד (faynd).

noun:Felge.tx: From Middle High German vëlge, from Old High German fëlga, from Proto-Germanic *felgō. Cognate with Dutch velg, English felly, felloe.

noun:Fetzen.tx: From Middle High German vetze (“rag, tatters”), ultimately from the root of fassen (“to grasp”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *fatą (“vat, item of clothing”), Old Norse fǫt (“clothes”), Portuguese fato (“clothing”), Spanish hato.

noun:Frage.tx: From Middle High German vrāge, from Old High German frāga, from Proto-West Germanic *frāgu, from Proto-Germanic *frēgō, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ-.

noun:Fieber.tx: From Middle High German fieber, from Old High German fiebar, from Proto-West Germanic *fēbr, borrowed from Latin febris (“fever”).

noun:Fink.tx: From Middle High German vinke, from Old High German finco.

noun:Fläche.tx: From Middle High German vleche, from Old High German flah, from Proto-West Germanic *flak, from Proto-Germanic *flakaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥keh (“flat surface”), found in the second element of English cromlech. Analysable as flach + -e (“ness”).

noun:Flachs.tx: From Middle High German vlahs, from Old High German flahs, from Proto-Germanic *flahsą (“flax”).

noun:Flagge.tx: Borrowed through Low German from English flag, or from early modern Dutch vlagghe. Compare contemporary Dutch vlag. See also Old Norse flǫgra and German flackern.

noun:Flaum.tx: From Middle High German phlūme, from Old High German phlūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmu (“down feather”). The modern onset f- instead of pf- is East Central German.

noun:Flaute.tx: From flau + -te, 18th century. See the former for more.

noun:Flechte.tx: From Middle High German vlehte. Compare Dutch vlecht, Gothic 𐍆𐌻𐌰𐌷𐍄𐌰 (flahta).

verb:flechten.tx: From Middle High German vlëhten, from Old High German flëhtan, from Proto-Germanic *flehtaną.

noun:Flegel.tx: From Middle High German vlegel, from Old High German flegil, from Proto-West Germanic *flagil, probably from Latin flagellum.

noun:Fliese.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German vlīse, from Proto-Germanic *flīsō (“split chip”), a nasalized dental extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”), whence also Proto-Germanic *splītaną (“to split”). Cognate with Swedish flis (“wood chips”) (DWDS).

noun:Flitter.tx: Back-formation from flittern, from Middle High German.

noun:Flinte.tx: Probably from Swedish flinta (borrowed during the Thirty Years's War). The word goes back to the ignition with a flint.

noun:Flocke.tx: From Old High German floccho. Cognate with English flake.

noun:Flotte.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German vlōte, which pertains to fließen (“to flow”). The contemporary form is modelled on French flotte.

noun:Fluch.tx: From Middle High German vluoch, from Old High German fluoh, deverbal from fluohhon. Cognate with Dutch vloek.

noun:Flur.tx: From Middle High German vluor, from Old High German fluor, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz. The word chiefly meant “arable land” in High German (see etymology 2). The modern sense was influenced or reinforced by Middle Low German vlōr. Cognate with Dutch vloer, English floor (from Old English flōr).

noun:Folge.tx: From Middle High German volge, from Old High German folga, from Proto-West Germanic *folgēn.

noun:Folter.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin poledrus (“a sharp-edged frame on which the suspect's feet were weighed down”), from Ancient Greek πῶλος (pôlos, “foal”).

noun:Forst.tx: From Middle High German forst~vorst, from Old High German forst, likely from Proto-West Germanic *furhiþi. Cognate with English forest.

noun:Frack.tx: 18th century, from English frock. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz and thus a doublet of Rock. The very open English [ɒ] was substituted with German [ɑ] (as it was then predominantly spoken).

noun:Friedhof.tx: From Middle High German vrīthof, from Old High German frīthof, derived from frīten (“to enclose”) + Hof (“yard”). In Early Modern German, the word came to be associated with the distantly related Frieden (“peace”), probably at first through interaction of diphthongising and non-diphthongising dialects, but then leading to semantic remotivation as “place of final peace”. Cognate with archaic Dutch vrijthof.

noun:Frist.tx: From Middle High German vrist, from Old High German frist, from Proto-Germanic *fristiz. Cognate with English frist, first. More at frist.

noun:Funke.tx: From Middle High German funke, vunke (also ablauted as vanke), from Old High German funko, funcho, from Proto-West Germanic *funkō, from Proto-Germanic *funkô. More at English spunk.

noun:Furche.tx: From Middle High German vurch, from Old High German furh, from Proto-West Germanic *furh, from Proto-Germanic *furhs. The word is an original root noun and shows rests of this declension in Middle High German alongside i-stem forms both with an without umlaut (vürhe, vurhe). From these, weak plurals (vürhen, vurhen) and new singulars in -e were later derived. Prevocalic -ch- < -h- is chiefly …

noun:Furcht.tx: From Middle High German vorht, vorhte, from Old High German forhta, forahta, from Proto-Germanic *furhtō (“fear”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥k- (“to fear”). The modern vowel -u- is due to influence by the related verb fürchten. Cognate with obsolete Dutch vrucht (still in godsvrucht), Middle Low German vruchte. Also closely related with English fright, though this is from a different stem …

noun:Fürst.tx: From Middle High German vürste, from Old High German furisto, from the substantivised weak inflection of Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first”). Calque of Latin prī̆nceps.

noun:Furt.tx: From Middle High German vurt m or (northern) f, from Old High German furt m, from Proto-West Germanic *furdu, from Proto-Germanic *furduz, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥téw-, oblique stem of *pértus. The feminine gender is of Central and Low German origin; compare Middle Low German vōrde m or f, whence also the doublet Förde f. Another doublet is Fjord, from Old Norse fjǫrðr. Further cognate with …

noun:Fladen.tx: From Middle High German vlade, flade, from Old High German flado, from Proto-West Germanic *flaþō.

noun:Fülle.tx: From Middle High German vülle, from Old High German fullī. Equivalent to voll + -e.

verb:fegen.tx: From Middle High German vëgen, from Old High German fëgōn, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn.

adj:froh.tx: From Middle High German vrō, from Old High German frō, frao, from Proto-Germanic *frawaz (“quick, glad”). Compare Dutch vrolijk, whence also English frolic.

verb:fesseln.tx: From Middle High German veȥȥeren, from Old High German feȥȥarōn. Synchronically analyzed as Fessel (“fetter, shackle”) + -n.

adj:fähig.tx: Variant of Middle High German gevæhic, from vāhen (“to catch”) (whence modern fangen). Thus originally “able to be comprehended”.

adj:faul.tx: From Middle High German vūl, from Old High German fūl, from Proto-West Germanic *fūl, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *puH-lo-s (“rotten, putrid”). Compare Dutch vuil, English foul, Danish ful, Swedish ful. Doublet of Foul. The sense “lazy” developed in part from the idea of food rotting when lying around, in part from the notion that idleness is morally rotten.

verb:fechten.tx: From Middle High German vëhten (“to fight”), from Old High German fëhtan (“to fight”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan, from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ-. Cognate to Low German fechten, Dutch vechten, English fight, Danish fægte, Norwegian Bokmål fekte, Norwegian Nynorsk fekta, fekte.

adj:fein.tx: From Middle High German fīn, from Old French fin, ultimately from Latin finis. See English fine for more.

adj:fertig.tx: From Middle High German fertec, from Old High German fartīg, from the noun fart (“journey”). Cognate with Dutch vaardig, Low German fardig, Old English fierd (“expedition, campaign”).

adj:flach.tx: From Middle High German vlach, from Old High German flah, from Proto-West Germanic *flak, from Proto-Germanic *flakaz.

verb:flehen.tx: From Middle High German vlēhen (also vlēgen, vlēn, etc.) from the coalescence of Old High German flēhan, flēhōn, flehōn, and flēgōn, from Proto-West Germanic *flaihijan, *flaihōn, *flaigōn (“to flatter”).

adj:flügge.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German vlügge in the 15th or 16th century, eventually completely displacing its High German equivalent flück, possibly motivated by better matching the consonantism of related fliegen.

verb:flüstern.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German vlisteren, ultimately of onomatopoetic origin. Related to Dutch fluisteren, Yiddish פֿליסטערן (flistern).

verb:fordern.tx: From Middle High German vodern/vordern, from Old High German fordarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *forþ(a)rōn. More at vorder.

verb:fördern.tx: From Middle High German vürdern, from Old High German furdiren, from Proto-West Germanic *furþrijan. Equivalent to archaic fürder (“further”) + -n. The modern ⟨ö⟩ corresponds to the variant förder, which probably developed through conflation with related vorder (whence fordern), but may have been reinforced by regular Middle Low German vȫrder, vȫrderen. Cognate with English further, which see.

verb:forschen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vorschen, from Old High German forscōn, from Proto-West Germanic *forskōn (“inquire, question”).

adj:fremd.tx: From Middle High German vremde, vremede, from Old High German fremidi, from Proto-West Germanic *framiþī. Cognate with English fremd, Dutch vreemd.

adj:fromm.tx: From Middle High German vrume (“efficient, good, righteous”), derived from Old High German fruma (“benefit”). The vocalism -o- could readily be explained as dialectal, but is already common in Middle High German. The commonest form in early modern German was frōm. Modern fromm is a variant with suppression of open-syllable lengthening (as commonly found before -m-). Related to Dutch vroom and Yiddish פֿרום (frum).

verb:freuen.tx: From Middle High German vrö(u)wen, vre(u)wen, from Old High German frewen, frouwen, a derivation of Old High German frō, frao (“glad”). Equivalent to froh (“glad”) + -en. Compare English frolic.

adj:frisch.tx: From Middle High German vrisch, from Old High German frisc, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-. Compare Dutch vers and fris, English fresh, Danish and Norwegian fersk, Swedish färsk. Doublet of Freske and Fresko.

adv:frisch.tx: From Middle High German vrisch, from Old High German frisc, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-. Compare Dutch vers and fris, English fresh, Danish and Norwegian fersk, Swedish färsk. Doublet of Freske and Fresko.

verb:frieren.tx: From Middle High German vrieren, vriesen, from Old High German friosan, from Proto-West Germanic *freusan, from Proto-Germanic *freusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *prews-. The -r- was generalised from the Middle High German past forms (as in verlieren). Cognate with German Low German freren, fresen, Dutch vriezen, English freeze, Danish fryse.

adj:früh.tx: From Middle High German vrüe, vrüeje, from Old High German fruoi, from Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī) (“early”). Cognate with Dutch vroeg, German Low German fröh, Saterland Frisian fröier (“formerly”).

adv:früh.tx: From Middle High German vrüe, vrüeje, from Old High German fruoi, from Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī) (“early”). Cognate with Dutch vroeg, German Low German fröh, Saterland Frisian fröier (“formerly”).

verb:fühlen.tx: From northern Middle High German vüelen (generally spelt vulen), from Old High German fuolen, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan (“to feel”), which see for cognates. Upper German dialects of Middle High German used enphinden instead. In Modern German, empfinden has been chiefly confined to higher register. Nevertheless many southern dialects still lack or avoid fühlen, usually preferring cognates of spüren.

verb:führen.tx: From Middle High German vüeren, from Old High German fuoren, from Proto-West Germanic *fōrijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną, originally the causative of faran (“to proceed”), modern fahren.

verb:füllen.tx: From Middle High German vüllen, from Old High German fullen. Compare Dutch vullen, English fill, Danish fylde, Swedish fylla.

adj:freundlich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vriuntlich, vrūntlich, friuntlich, from Old High German friuntlīh, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndlīkaz, equivalent to Freund + -lich. Cognate with Dutch vriendelijk, English friendly.

noun:Freundschaft.tx: From Middle High German vriuntschaft, from Old High German friuntscaf, from Proto-West Germanic *friundskapi. Equivalent to Freund (“friend”) + -schaft (“-ship”).

noun:Frische.tx: From Middle High German vrische; equivalent to frisch + -e.

verb:firmen.tx: From Middle High German firmen, from Old High German firmōn, from Latin firmāre.

verb:formen.tx: From Middle High German formen, equivalent to Form + -en.

adj:funktionell.tx: From French fonctionnel, from fonction (“function”), equivalent to funktion + -ell. Cognate with Dutch functioneel, Danish funktionel, Norwegian funksjonell and Swedish funktionell.

noun:Fries.tx: Borrowed from French frise, from an Upper Italian fris f.

adj:fantastisch.tx: From Latin phantasticus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch. By surface analysis, Fantast (“fantasist, dreamer”) + -isch.

adj:folgend.tx: From Middle High German volgende, from Old High German folgēnto, from Proto-West Germanic *folgēndī, from Proto-Germanic *fulgāndz. By surface analysis, folgen + -end. Piecewise doublet of followend.

noun:Florett.tx: Borrowed from French fleuret, from Italian fioretto (“little flower”).

noun:Fräulein.tx: Middle High German vrouwelīn (“mistress, young unmarried noblewoman”), equivalent to Frau + -lein.

noun:Festplatte.tx: fest (“solid, hard”) + Platte (“disk”), calque of English hard disk.

adj:fällig.tx: From Middle High German vellic, vellec, from Old High German fellīg (“staggering, dilapidated, inclined to fall, obliged to yield or pay”), equivalent to Fall + -ig. Cognate with Middle Low German vellich, Middle Dutch vellich, vallich.

noun:Fasan.tx: From Middle High German fasān, fasant, alteration after Old French fasan(t) of older fashuon, from Old High German fasihuon, itself an alteration based on huon (“chicken”) of unattested *fasiān, from Latin phasianus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós).

adj:feminin.tx: In the grammatical sense (since 15th c.) from Latin fēminīnus. Broader use (chiefly since 19th c.) after French féminin.

verb:fälschen.tx: From Middle High German velschen, valschen, from Old High German falskōn, falsken, from Proto-West Germanic *falskōn.

adj:friedlich.tx: From Middle High German vridelich; equivalent to Frieden + -lich. Cognate with Luxembourgish friddlech.

noun:Frequenz.tx: Borrowed from Latin frequentia (“crowd, multitude, throng”).

noun:Faschismus.tx: From Italian fascismo, from Latin fasces.

noun:Frisur.tx: 18th century, from French frisure (“curly hairdo, frisure”).

noun:Ferne.tx: From fern. Compare Low German Feren, dative, as in in sikerer Feren and in rhyme to Steren (pl.).

adj:fanatisch.tx: Borrowed from French fanatique, from Latin fānāticus.

noun:Fehde.tx: From Middle High German vēhede, vēde, from Old High German fēhida, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“hatred, enmity”).

noun:Fotografie.tx: Ultimately from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + γράφω (gráphō, “I write”), possibly influenced by English photography

adj:fragwürdig.tx: From fragen (“to ask”) + -würdig (“-worthy”), commonly associated with August Wilhelm Schlegel's translation of Shakespeare's Hamlet.

verb:foltern.tx: From Late Middle High German foltern. Equivalent to Folter + -en.

verb:fluchen.tx: From Middle High German vluochen, from Old High German fluohhon, from Proto-West Germanic *flōkan, from Proto-Germanic *flōkaną. Cognate with Dutch vloeken.

noun:Fron.tx: From Middle High German vrōn(e) (“rule, lordship”), from vrōn (“holy”, literally “belonging to Gods”), from Old High German frōno (“(possession) of the gods”), genitive plural of frō (“Lord, God”), from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjō.

adj:fidel.tx: From Latin fidēlis, from the noun fidēs.

adj:fröhlich.tx: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz. By surface analysis, froh + -lich. Cognate to Low German froihlik (frauh + -lik) (Paderbornisch).

noun:Felsen.tx: From Middle High German felse, fels, from Old High German fels m (8. c), felis m (8. c), feliso m (8. c), felisa f (9. c), possibly from Proto-West Germanic *falis (“rock, cliff”), whence Old Saxon felis, Middle Dutch vels. Pfeifer is uncertain about the further origin. In one theory, he mentions the comparison to Old Norse fjall, Swedish fjäll, Sanskrit पाषाण (pāṣāṇá), Ancient Greek πέλλα …

noun:Fleischer.tx: From Middle High German fleischer, vleischer, vleischære, equivalent to Fleisch + -er. Compare also Old High German fleiskskerni (“butcher”).

noun:Feinschmecker.tx: From fein (“fine, good”) + Schmecker (“taster”); see schmecken (“to taste”) for more on the latter component's origin.

verb:feuern.tx: From Feuer. The sense “terminate employment” is a semantic loan from English.

adj:furchtbar.tx: From Middle High German vorhtebære. Equivalent to Furcht + -bar.

adv:furchtbar.tx: From Middle High German vorhtebære. Equivalent to Furcht + -bar.

adj:fadenscheinig.tx: From older fadenschein, corresponding to Faden (“thread”) + Schein (“appearance”).

noun:Feuerzeug.tx: By surface analysis, Feuer (“fire”) + Zeug (“stuff”) / erzeugen (“to create”). Historically, from Middle High German viurziuc.

noun:Faustregel.tx: Since at least the end of the 19th century. From Faust (“fist”) + Regel (“rule”). The semantic development is unknown.

noun:Feuchtigkeit.tx: feucht + -igkeit. Compare Danish fugtighed, Dutch vochtigheid, Swedish fuktighet and Norwegian Bokmål fuktighet.

noun:Fleischfresser.tx: From Fleisch (“meat”) + Fresser (“eater”). At least in the scientific sense a calque of Latin carnivorus and sarcophagus.

noun:Fauxpas.tx: Unadapted borrowing from French faux pas.

adj:furchtsam.tx: From Middle High German vorhtesam (“fearful; fearsome”). Equivalent to Furcht (“fear”) + -sam (“-some”).

verb:fiebern.tx: Late Middle High German fiebern, equivalent to Fieber + -en.

noun:Forschung.tx: From Middle High German vorschunge, from Old High German forskunga, from Proto-West Germanic *forskungu, equivalent to forschen (“to research”) + -ung.

noun:Fantasie.tx: From Middle High German fantasīe (whence also the obsolete doublet Phantasei), learned borrowing from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰσῐ́ᾱ (phăntăsĭ́ā). Doublet of fancy and Fantasia.

verb:feiern.tx: From Middle High German vīren, from Old High German fīrōn, derived from fīra, whence modern Feier. Compare Dutch vieren.

noun:Feudalismus.tx: From feudal + -ismus [early 19th century], from Medieval Latin feudālis, from Latin feudum n (“fief, fee”).

noun:Fixer.tx: Borrowed from English fixer or from fixen + -er.

verb:frisieren.tx: From French friser, possibly through Dutch friseren.

noun:Fiasko.tx: Borrowed from Italian fiasco (literally “bottle”), from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of Flakon and Flasche.

noun:Furz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vurz, from Old High German furz, from Proto-West Germanic *furtu, from Proto-Germanic *furtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-.

adj:feige.tx: From Middle High German veige, from Old High German feigi (“appointed for death, ungodly”), from Proto-West Germanic *faigī (“cowardly, wicked, fey, doomed to die”). Cognate with Dutch veeg (“dying, doomed, perilous, cowardly”), English fey (“doomed to die”).

adv:feige.tx: From Middle High German veige, from Old High German feigi (“appointed for death, ungodly”), from Proto-West Germanic *faigī (“cowardly, wicked, fey, doomed to die”). Cognate with Dutch veeg (“dying, doomed, perilous, cowardly”), English fey (“doomed to die”).

noun:Fasson.tx: Late 15th century, borrowed from Middle French fa­çon.

noun:Frömmigkeit.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]. Structurally, fromm + -igkeit

noun:Fernrohr.tx: Compound of fern (“far”) + Rohr (“tube”), a loose calque of Dutch verrekijker.

noun:Florist.tx: From Flora + -ist, probably after French fleuriste.

noun:Fäustling.tx: From Middle High German viustelinc, from Old High German fūstiling. Equivalent to Faust + -ling.

noun:Fabrik.tx: Borrowed from Latin fābrica or French fabrique.

verb:färben.tx: From Middle High German verwen, from Old High German farawen, from the root of Farbe (“color, dye, paint”).

noun:Fabrikat.tx: Borrowed from Latin fabricātus, perfect passive participle of fabricō (“frame, build, forge”), from fabrica (“a fabric, building, etc.”).

adj:flüssig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vlüȥȥic, vlüȥȥec, from Middle High German fluzzīg. By surface analysis, Fluss + -ig.

verb:fauchen.tx: From Middle High German pfūchen, phūchen, from Old High German *pfūhhan (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Germanic *pukaną (“to spit, puff”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). The modern onset f- instead of pf- is from East Central German. Compare English puke.

noun:Feldherr.tx: Compound of Feld (“field”) + Herr (“master”). Compare Dutch veldheer.

noun:Feldwebel.tx: From earlier Feldweibel, a compound of Feld (“field”) + Weibel (“usher”). The modern vocalism is East Central German, probably standardised (outside Switzerland) to avoid the resemblance to Weib (“woman, wife”).

noun:Finne.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German finne, vinne, from Old Saxon *finna, from Proto-Germanic *finnō. More at fin.

noun:Franzose.tx: From Middle High German franzōse, franzoise, from Old French françois.

verb:faulenzen.tx: From Middle High German vūlezen (originally “to rot”), which is derived from the predecessor of German faul (“rotten; lazy”) with an intensifying suffix -ezzen (see Proto-Germanic *-atjaną). Later on -n- was infixed, either caused by or causing an association with Lenz (“spring-time”, and hence “time of joy”). Compare also the expression ein lauer Lenz (“a period of idleness”).

adj:farbig.tx: From Farbe (“color”) + -ig. In the sense relating to skin color a calque of English colored.

adj:forsch.tx: Via German Low German [Term?] from Middle Low German fors (“brisk, bold”), derived from forse, which is borrowed from Old French force. The development -rs → -rsch is frequent in modern German (see Arsch). Compare Dutch fors.

noun:Fuhrmann.tx: From Fuhre (“cargo, wagonload”) + Mann (“man”). Compare Vormann, Dutch voorman.

noun:Fuchsschwanz.tx: From Middle High German vuhsswanz, from Middle Low German vosswanz. By surface analysis, Fuchs (“fox”) + Schwanz (“tail”).

adj:freiwillig.tx: From Late Middle High German freywillic (1370s), but common chiefly since the 16th century. By surface analysis, frei (“free”) + willig (“willing”), perhaps after freier Wille (“free will”). Compare Dutch vrijwillig (1390s).

noun:Fazit.tx: 15th century, from Latin facit (“it makes, comes down to”).

noun:Flakon.tx: Borrowed from French flacon. Doublet of Fiasko and Flasche.

noun:Fernsehsender.tx: Compound of fernseh(en) (“to watch television”) + Sender (“broadcaster, transmitter”).

noun:Filiale.tx: Borrowed from Latin fīliālis (“filial”) (DWDS), as branches of an organization are akin to "sons and daughters" of the organization.

noun:Freudenhaus.tx: From Freude (“joy”) + -en- + Haus (“house”). Compare French maison de joie.

noun:Fingerhut.tx: From Middle High German fingerhuot, vingerhuot, equivalent to Finger (“finger”) + Hut (“hood”). Cognate with German Low German Fingerhood (“thimble”), Dutch vingerhoed (“thimble”), Saterland Frisian Fingerhoud (“thimble”), West Frisian fingerhoed (“thimble”).

verb:feilschen.tx: From Middle High German veilschen, from earlier veilsen, from Old High German *feilisōn, derived from feili, whence modern feil (“vendible”), which see.

verb:furzen.tx: From Middle High German vurzen, from Old High German furzen, from Proto-West Germanic *furtijan.

noun:Fegefeuer.tx: From Middle High German vëgeviur, a calque of Latin īgnis pūrgātōrius or īgnis pūrgātiōnis. By surface analysis, fegen + Feuer. Compare Dutch vagevuur.

verb:fahnden.tx: From Middle High German vanden, from Old High German fantōn, from Proto-Germanic *fandōną (“to find out”), from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass, bridge”). The lengthening of the vowel is irregular; compare ahnden.

noun:Fürstentum.tx: From Middle High German vürst(en)tuom. Equivalent to Fürst + -en- + -tum. Compare Silesian firsztyntōm (“duchy”).

adv:freilich.tx: From Middle High German vrīlīche(n), from Old High German frīlīhhēn (“freely, without fear or inhibition”). By surface analysis, frei (“free”) + -lich (“-ly”).

noun:Fritten.tx: Shortened from Pommes frites and provided with a German plural. The abbreviation may have been under the direct influence of French frites, since the more widespread short form (outside of western Germany) is Pommes.

adj:fies.tx: Spread during the 20th century from Low German, Low Franconian, and Central Franconian dialects, from Middle Low German vīs and early modern Dutch vijs, respectively. Compare contemporary Dutch vies (from a dialectal form), West Frisian fiis. Per Pfeifer a connection with Latin spīrō (“to breathe, blow”) is possible.

noun:Fußgänger.tx: From Middle High German vuozgenger, from Old High German [Term?]; compare Dutch voetganger. Fuß + Gänger.

verb:feilen.tx: From Middle High German vīlen, Old High German fīhalōn, ultimately from the root of Feile (“tool for smoothing a hard material”).

verb:flankieren.tx: Borrowed from French flanquer. By surface analysis, Flanke + -ieren.

noun:Fortschritt.tx: From fort- + Schritt, a calque of Latin prōgressus. See also fortschreiten.

noun:Förster.tx: From Middle High German forster, Old High German forstāri, compare Forst.

noun:Floskel.tx: 17th century, from Latin flosculus (“flowery expression”). The feminine singular is a backformation from the plural.

noun:Feldbett.tx: Originally used in the military; from Feld (“warzone”) + Bett (“bed”)

noun:Folklore.tx: Borrowed from English folklore with a spelling pronunciation. Doublet of Volklehre; not to be confused with Volkslehre (“ethnology”), a term now associated with Nazism.

verb:filtrieren.tx: From Latin filtrare, equivalent to Filter + -ieren.

noun:Fehlschlag.tx: fehl- + Schlag Compare the noun Fehlschlagen, nominalisation of the verb fehlschlagen

verb:flüchten.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vlühten, from Old High German fluhten (“to chase off, drive away”), which the meaning shifting from making others flee to fleeing oneself. By surface analysis, Flucht + -en, and thereby ultimately related to fliehen.

noun:Faktor.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin factor, factōris.

adj:flexibel.tx: From Latin flexibilis, from flectere (“to bend”).

noun:Finanz.tx: Back-formation from Finanzen, from French finance(s).

verb:flicken.tx: From Middle High German vlicken, denominal from vlëc = Modern Fleck, “to apply flecks to”.

adj:flüchtig.tx: From Middle High German vlühtic, vlüchtec, from Old High German fluhtīg. By surface analysis, Flucht + -ig. Cognate with Dutch vluchtig.

verb:frohlocken.tx: From Middle High German vrōlocken (“rejoice”). Cognate with Dutch vrolijk (“joyous”), English frolic.

noun:Fug.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vuoc (“propriety, that which is opportune”).

noun:Fruchtbarkeit.tx: fruchtbar + -keit. Compare Dutch vruchtbaarheid, Swedish fruktbarhet, Danish frugtbarhed.

noun:Flohmarkt.tx: Probably a calque of French marché aux puces, possibly via English flea market. By surface analysis, Floh (“flea”) + Markt (“market”).

pt: a measure of beer or wine
noun:Frühschoppen.tx: From früh (“early”) + Schoppen (“a measure of beer or wine”).

noun:Favorit.tx: Borrowed from Middle French favorit (“favored one”), from favorir (“to favor”), from Latin favor (“good will, favor”).

verb:fixen.tx: The verb is borrowed from English fix + -en.

noun:Festung.tx: From Middle High German vestunge, from vesten (“to fasten, to secure”), from Old High German festen, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz (“firm, secure”). Compare Dutch vesting, English fastness (“fortress”).

verb:fingieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin fingere. Cognate with English feign.

verb:fachen.tx: 15th century, at first predominantly in the form fochen. Usually derived from Medieval Latin focō, itself from Latin focus (“hearth”). The -ch- is problematic, however. If it were due to the High German consonant shift, the word would have to be 700 years older than its first attestation. It should not be ruled out that fach, foch may be onomatopoeias for the ignition of a fire and/or the stoker's blowing.

adj:feil.tx: From Middle High German veile, from Old High German feili (“for sale”), from Proto-West Germanic *failī. Possibly merged with a descendant of Proto-Germanic *falaz, but this is uncertain. Old High German fali is only attested once in a text that uses ai for ei, thus quite plausibly a mere scribal error (regarding also that short a should be umlauted to e). Cognate with Dutch veil. From *falaz …

noun:Flexibilität.tx: Borrowed from French flexibilité, from Late Latin flexibilitās, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). By surface analysis, flexibel + -ität.

noun:Fährmann.tx: From northern Middle High German verman (14th c.). By surface analysis, Fähre (“ferry”) + Mann (“man”). Compare Middle Dutch and Middle Low German vērman (both also 14th c.), modern Dutch veerman.

noun:Füchsin.tx: From Middle High German vühsinne, from Old High German *fuhsinna, from Proto-West Germanic *fuhsini, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsinī. By surface analysis, Fuchs + -in. Cognate with English vixen.

adj:fotogen.tx: From English photogenic, equivalent to Foto + -gen.

noun:Fernglas.tx: Compound of fern (“far”) + Glas (“glass”), a loose calque of Dutch verrekijker.

adj:formell.tx: Borrowed from French formel, from Latin fōrmālis. Doublet of formal.

noun:Fastnacht.tx: From Middle High German vastnaht, from vaste (“fast”) + naht (“night”). Cognate with Silesian East Central German Foasnacht, Mòcheno Vosnòcht.

adj:febril.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris.

pron:frau.tx: From Frau by making the first letter lower-case. Coined as an alternative to the male-sounding word man (“one”), which is cognate and homophonous with Mann (“adult male”). First used by feminists when writing about women, then occasionally used in general contexts. Compare the pronoun mensch. Compare also the use of she vs he in English to refer to someone whose gender is unknown.

verb:formieren.tx: From Middle High German formieren, from Old French former and Latin fōrmāre. By surface analysis, Form + -ieren.

phrase:Feuer frei.tx: Literally, “fire free”, or more loosely translated as “fire is permitted”.

noun:Föhn.tx: From Old High German phonno, from Vulgar Latin faōnius, an alteration of Latin favōnius (“west wind”), from Latin Favōnius (“Favonius”), a Roman wind god.

noun:Fassung.tx: From Middle High German fazzunge, vazzunge, from Old High German fazzunga, equivalent to fassen + -ung. Cognate with Middle Low German vātinge.

noun:Folie.tx: Borrowed from Vulgar Latin folia, plural of folium, since the 16th century.

noun:Fremder.tx: From fremd + -er. Compare Low German Frümeder (en Frümeder, dei Frümede).

noun:Fluse.tx: Borrowed from Low German Fluse, from Middle Low German vlūs (“sheepskin”) or a derivative thereof, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *fleus (“fleece”). The same word from an earlier borrowing is Flause (“illusion”), making these doublets along with Flausch.

pt: to flutter, glitter, giggle, flatter, caress
noun:Flittchen.tx: Probably from underlying *Flitterchen, from flittern (“to flutter, glitter, giggle, flatter, caress”) + -chen, or alternatively from the related noun Flitter (“lustre, glitter, cheap jewellery, vanity”).

noun:Findling.tx: From Middle High German vundelinc (“foundling”), equivalent to modern Fund (“a find, finding”) + -ling; later altered after the verb finden (“to find”). The Middle High German form corresponds exactly to Middle Dutch vondelinc (whence Dutch vondeling), Middle Low German vundelink, Middle English fundeling (whence English foundling). These terms may be cognate through West Germanic, though it is …

verb:fummeln.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German fummelen, fimmelen, perhaps ultimately imitative of fumbling. Or, from Proto-Indo-European *pal- (“to shake, swing”), see also Latin palpō (“to pat, touch softly”), and possibly Proto-Germanic *fōlijaną (“to feel”). Cognate with English fumble.

noun:Firnis.tx: From Middle High German firnîs, vernîʒ, from Old French vernis.

verb:formulieren.tx: Borrowed from French formuler, ultimately from Latin fōrmula (“a small pattern or mold, form, rule, principle, method, formula”), diminutive of forma (“a form”); whence Form.

noun:Faxe.tx: From a shortening of dialectal Fickesfackes (“nonsense, silly jokes”), from fickfacken (“to push back and forth, fuck around”), a reduplication of ficken (“to fuck”). Alternatively a derivative of obsolete fatzen (“to fool, make a fool of, mock”), from Middle High German fatzen (“to fool”).

noun:Fraß.tx: From Middle High German vrāȥ, from Old High German frāȥ, from Proto-Germanic *fr(a)ētaz, derived from *fr(a)etaną, whence German fressen (“to eat”). Cognate with Dutch vraat.

noun:Forke.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German vorke, from Old Saxon furka, from Proto-West Germanic *furkō, from Latin furca. The word did originally exist in High German (already Old High German furka), but the modern use is based on the Low German lineage and chiefly restricted to originally Low German areas. Compare Dutch vork, English fork.

noun:Fresko.tx: Borrowed from Italian fresco. Doublet of Freske and frisch.

noun:Freske.tx: Borrowed from French fresque. Doublet of Fresko and frisch.

noun:Freibad.tx: frei (“free”) + Bad (“bath, pool”), in the sense of "free" as "unrestricted", i.e. outdoors.

noun:Freistoß.tx: frei + Stoß, modeled after English free kick.

adj:flämisch.tx: From Middle High German vlæmisch, flemisch. By surface analysis, Flame + -isch.

verb:funkeln.tx: From Middle High German vunkeln, iterative of vunken (“to spark”), derived from the noun vunke, whence modern Funke(n) (“a spark”). By surface analysis, funken + -eln. Cognate with Dutch fonkelen, Middle Low German vunkeln (“to sparkle”).

noun:Frettchen.tx: Diminutive of an obsolete simplex frett, which is borrowed via Middle Dutch furet, fret from Old French furet, + -chen. Compare modern Dutch fret.

adv:flugs.tx: From Middle High German vluges, adverbial genitive from vluc, whence modern Flug (“flight, flying”). Equivalent to Flug + -s. Compare Dutch vlug (“quickly”), which is a related, though not identical word, and fluks, which originates in Middle Dutch but is in its modern form influenced by German.

noun:Feste.tx: From Middle High German veste, from Old High German festī. Equivalent to fest (“fast, secure”) + -e (“-th, -ness”), compare similar English fastness.

verb:foppen.tx: Uncertain, perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch focken (“to breed; to fuck; to tease”) with uncommon sound development of [k] to [p] (influenced either by the preceding rounded vowel or assimilation to the /f/), from Old Dutch *fokkon, from Proto-West Germanic *fukkōn, possibly from Proto-Germanic *fukkōną (“to strike, copulate”). Compare modern Dutch fokken. However, note older Middle English …

adj:flott.tx: Via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch vlot (“afloat, floatable”). Ultimately from the root of fließen (“to flow”).

verb:feien.tx: From Fei (Fey) (obsolete variant of Fee (“fairy”)) + -en, implying invincibility by magic.

noun:Freier.tx: From freien (“to woo, to exhibit love”). Semantic pejoration is also found, to a lesser extent, in Dutch vrijen (now generally “to have sex”).

noun:Fernsprecher.tx: From fern (“far”) + Sprecher (“speaker”). Compare English farspeaker.

noun:Fallrückzieher.tx: From Fall (“fall”) + Rückzieher (“act of pulling back”). Further analysable as Fall + rück- + ziehen + -er.

noun:Fußspur.tx: From Middle High German vuozspor, from Old High German fuozspor, from Proto-West Germanic *fōtspor, from Proto-Germanic *fōtspurą, equivalent to Fuß + Spur.

verb:faulen.tx: From Middle High German fūlen, vūlen, from Old High German fūlēn, from Proto-West Germanic *fūlijan (“to become foul; rot; decay”).

verb:flitzen.tx: From obsolete Flitz (“arrow”) + -en, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, from Frankish *fliukkijā, related to *fleugan (“to fly”) (whence fliegen), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-.

verb:flutschen.tx: From German Low German fluschen. Compare Saterland Frisian flutskje, English flush.

verb:freien.tx: Originally restricted to Low and Central German; generalized by Luther. Borrowed from Middle Low German vrien and Middle High German vrīen, frīen, vrijen, vrigen, from Old High German *frīon; compare Old Saxon friohon. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frijōną. Cognate to Dutch vrijen.

noun:Frust.tx: Clipping of Frustration, from Latin frūstrātiō.

noun:Fiffi.tx: From a pet name, probably from an onomatopoeia for whistling. Compare dialectal fifi (interjection used to indicate that the seeker in a game of hide-and-seek may now start their search). See also Luxembourgish Fiffi below.

noun:Franke.tx: From Middle High German Franke, from Old High German Franko, from Frankish *Franko, from Proto-Germanic *frankô.

noun:Frachtschiff.tx: Fracht (“freight”) + Schiff (“ship”), after Middle Low German vrachtschip.

verb:flittern.tx: Middle High German flettern, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flutrōną, frequentative of *flutōną (“to float”). Probably related to Low German fluttern. Cognate with English flutter and related to English float.

noun:Fibel.tx: 15th century, from a popular (perhaps childish) dissimilation of Bibel (“bible”). Primers were originally based on passages from the Bible.

noun:Fenn.tx: From Middle Low German venne, from Old Saxon fenni, from Proto-West Germanic *fani, from Proto-Germanic *fanją. The word did exist in High German (Old High German fenni), but Middle High German venne is rare and the word was later lost in Upper German and most dialects of Central German. The modern form is therefore based chiefly on the Low German lineage. Cognate with Dutch veen, Walloon fagne …

noun:Fasching.tx: From Middle High German vaschanc, vaschang, from a conflation of unattested Old High German *vastganc (“exuberant goings-on at a carnival”) (exact cognate of Old English fastgang (“fasting; Shrove Tuesday”)) and *vastschanc (“serving of the fasting drink, esp. before the start of Lent”) (from a component *vast related to Proto-Germanic *fastāną (“to observe, fast, abstain”) + Schank (“a giving”)), + a suffix -ing.

noun:Feierabend.tx: From Feier (“celebration”) + Abend (“evening”) or feiern (“to celebrate”) + Abend (“evening”). Originally related to Vorabend (“evening before”), it took on its current meaning in the 16th century.

adv:fürwahr.tx: From Middle High German vür + wār, by surface analysis, für + wahr. Compare similarly formed zwar.

noun:Flammkuchen.tx: Flamme + Kuchen. Compare Alsatian and Alemannic German Flammekueche, French flammekueche.

adj:fleißig.tx: From Middle High German vlīȥic, vlīȥec, from Old High German flīȥīg. By surface analysis, Fleiß + -ig.

adv:fleißig.tx: From Middle High German vlīȥic, vlīȥec, from Old High German flīȥīg. By surface analysis, Fleiß + -ig.

adj:familiär.tx: From French familier, from Latin familiāris, equivalent to Familie + -är.

noun:Feuerwehrfrau.tx: From Feuerwehr (“fire brigade”) + Frau (“woman”), in analogy to Feuerwehrmann (“fireman, male firefighter”).

verb:futtern.tx: From Middle High German vuotern, old variant of füttern, which see. Semantic split since the 19th century.

verb:fetten.tx: From Middle High German vetten, fetten (“to make fat”), partially from Old High German fatōn (“to nourish, feed, make fat”), from Proto-West Germanic *fadōn (“to nourish, feed, graze”), partially equivalent to Fett + -en. Cognate with German Low German fetten (“to smear”), Old English fadian (“to lead, guide, arrange”).

verb:feuchten.tx: From Middle High German viuhten, from Old High German fūhten, from the adjective fūht, fūhti. By surface analysis, feucht + -en. In modern usage almost exclusively with prefixes.

noun:Fraktion.tx: Borrowed from French fraction, from Latin fractiō.

noun:Frauenzimmer.tx: From Middle High German vrouwenzimmer; Frau (“woman”) + -en- + Zimmer (“room”). Originally (in the 15th century) denoting a woman's room, then her things and (in the 16th century) her attendants, and then (in the 17th century) an individual woman, often one of low status, for which reason the term started to become derogatory. Compare Danish fruentimmer and Swedish fruntimmer.

verb:fertigen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vertigen, vertegen (“to prepare, make ready, keep ready”). By surface analysis, fertig + -en.

noun:Fließ.tx: From Middle High German vliez, from Old High German flioz, from Proto-West Germanic *fleut, from Proto-Germanic *fleutą. Doublet of Fleet. Related with fließen, Fluss.

adv:folgendermaßen.tx: Univerbation of folgender (“following”) + Maßen (“measure”), an adverbial genitive of a mostly-obsolete feminine form of Maß, compare dermaßen.

verb:frommen.tx: From Middle High German vrumen, from Old High German frummen, *frumen. Related to the adjective fromm.

noun:Feuchte.tx: Inherited from Middle High German viuhte, from Old High German fūhtī; equivalent to feucht + -e (“-ness”).

adv:fürbass.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vürbaz, from Old High German furibaz. By surface analysis, für + bass.

noun:Firmament.tx: From Middle High German firmament, from Late Latin firmāmentum.

adj:folgerichtig.tx: Folge (“consequence”) + richtig (“correct, correctly”). Coined in the 19th century as a translation for French conséquent.

adv:folgerichtig.tx: Folge (“consequence”) + richtig (“correct, correctly”). Coined in the 19th century as a translation for French conséquent.

noun:Fachhochschule.tx: From Fach (“field of study, subject”) + Hochschule (“college, university”).

noun:Fut.tx: Inherited from Middle High German vut.

verb:flöhen.tx: From Floh + -en. Compare Cimbrian vlöogan, Dutch vlooien.

noun:Flehen.tx: From flehen, from Old High German flēhan.

noun:Fuhrwerk.tx: From late Middle High German vuorwërc, fūrwërc, equivalent to Fuhre + Werk.

phrase:Friede, Freude, Eierkuchen.tx: Literally, “peace, joy, pancakes”. The origin of the phrase is uncertain; it is attested in print at least since 1959, when the critic Carl Andrießen wrote, “Am Schluß, wie sichs gehört, Friede, Freude, Eierkuchen und Beifall” (‘At the end, as is proper, peace, joy, pancakes, and applause’).

noun:Fundament.tx: From Middle High German fundament, from Old High German fundament, from Latin fundāmentum.

noun:Funktionär.tx: Calque of French fonctionnaire; from Funktion + -är.

noun:Football.tx: Borrowed from English football. Doublet of the calque Fußball (“association football”).

noun:Fachliteratur.tx: Compound of Fach + Literatur. Compare Dutch vakliteratuur.

noun:Falkner.tx: From Middle High German valkenære, probably after Latin falconarius. Equivalent to Falke + -n- + -er.

verb:flackern.tx: From Middle High German vlackern, perhaps ultimately imitative of birds' wings, or from Proto-Germanic *flakuraz (“shaking, wavering”), related to *flakurōną (“to roam, wander”), from Proto-Indo-European *plag- (“to roam, wander”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelə- (“to wander”). Or, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”). From flacken + -ern (iterative suffix) See also West Frisian flikkerje, …

noun:Fehlbetrag.tx: fehl- + Betrag See also fehlen in the sense of “to lack”.

noun:Fimmel.tx: A dialectal word that spread supraregionally during the 20th century. It has not been established in the etymological literature which dialects are at the origin, but they seem to be those of what is now North Rhine-Westphalia. The Rheinisches Wörterbuch (20th century) stated that the word was common throughout Ripuarian and Low Franconian, but had only begun to spread to Moselle Franconian. The …

noun:Fischerei.tx: From Middle High German fischerīe, vischerīe, equivalent to Fisch + -erei. Compare Middle Dutch visscherie (modern Dutch visserij), Middle Low German vischærīe (modern German Low German Fiskeree (East Frisian)), English fishery.

noun:Fauteuil.tx: Unadapted borrowing from French fauteuil, eventually from Proto-West Germanic *faldistōl. Doublet of Faldistorium and Faltstuhl.

verb:flattern.tx: Early New High German flatern, from Middle High German vladeren, probably related to Falter (“moth”). Compare Dutch fladderen, Lithuanian plazdė́ti (“to flutter, beat the wings vigorously”), Latvian pledināt (“to move the wings”).

noun:Furunkel.tx: Borrowed from Latin fūrunculus (“a petty thief, pilferer; a pointed burning sore, boil”), diminutive of fūr (“a thief”).

noun:Feme.tx: From northern Middle High German veme, a borrowing from Middle Low German vēme. Cognate with Dutch veem. The further origin is unknown, though a relation with either Fehde (“feud”) or Feind (“enemy”) has been considered.

adj:flapsig.tx: From Flaps (“lout, oaf, churl”) + -ig, ultimately from flapp, imitative of the sound of clapping. Further meanings developed in the German Low German [Term?] and Central German dialects and vernaculars. Compare German Flappe (“twisted mouth, hanging bottom lip”).

verb:flirren.tx: Borrowed from German Low German flirren, of onomatopoeic origin.

noun:Flitz.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German flitse, flitsche, Dutch flitse, both borrowed from Middle French fleche (“arrow”), from Vulgar Latin *fleccia.

verb:flunkern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. The original meaning is “to gleam, move quickly”. Compare flink. The meaning “to boast, stretch the truth” (probably from “want to shine, be brilliant”) already developed in Low German.

verb:fluppen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?] and Central German dialects. Compare with English flop, Dutch floppen.

noun:Förde.tx: From Low German Föörd(e) (“ford, shallow water, firth”), from Middle Low German vȫrde, byform (perhaps originally plural) of vōrt, from Proto-Germanic *furduz. Doublet of inherited Furt (“ford, river passage”) and of Fjord (“fjord”), from Old Norse fjǫrðr. This latter may also have influenced the sense of the Low German.

noun:Freibeuter.tx: First attested 1579. Borrowed from Dutch vrijbuiter (1572, but older). Analysable as frei (“free”) + Beute (“booty”) + -er.

noun:Fussel.tx: From Middle High German visel m or f. The modern form with -u- is a Central German variant. Further origin unknown. Probably related to German Faser. Compare in particular Dutch vezel.

adj:flau.tx: Via Middle Low German flau, from Middle Dutch vlau (compare modern Dutch flauw). The Dutch word was borrowed from Old French flou (“tired, weary”), which is probably of Germanic origin and, if so, then cognate with German lau.

verb:flammen.tx: From Middle High German vlammen. Equivalent to Flamme + -en.

noun:Fernsehprediger.tx: Calque of English televangelist, from fernsehen + Prediger.

noun:Fuffi.tx: From Fuffziger + -i, from fuffzig, variant of fünfzig (“fifty”).

verb:ferngucken.tx: fern + gucken, by analogy to fernsehen.

noun:Freidenker.tx: frei + Denker, calque of English freethinker.

noun:Frühe.tx: From Late Middle High German früe (15th century), older *vrüeje, from Old High German fruoī, derived from Proto-West Germanic *frō (“early”). By surface analysis, früh + -e.

verb:fortschreiten.tx: fort- + schreiten, a calque of Latin prōgredior

noun:Fleece.tx: Borrowed from English fleece. Doublet of Vlies.

noun:Freitod.tx: frei (“free”) + Tod (“death”). Calque of Latin mors voluntāria.

noun:Firmung.tx: Middle High German firmunge, by surface analysis, firmen + -ung.

noun:Fiedel.tx: From Middle High German videle, from Old High German fidula, Proto-West Germanic *fiþulā (“fiddle”). Cognate with English fiddle.

noun:Fortune.tx: Borrowed from French fortune, from Latin fortuna.

noun:Fallreep.tx: Via German Low German [Term?] from Dutch valreep (attested 1612). Analysable as fallen (“to fall”) + Reep (“rope”).

adj:frostig.tx: From Middle High German vrostec, from Old High German frostag, from Proto-West Germanic *frostag, from Proto-Germanic *frustagaz, equivalent to Frost + -ig.

noun:Feudel.tx: Borrowed from Low German Feudel, Feul, Feil, either from or cognate with Dutch feil (“floorcloth”, attested 1616). Further origin uncertain. Ripuarian Fuddel (“old rag”), if related, would suggest that the d is original, whereas all of the following theories require that it is due to hypercorrection: * From Old French faille (“headscarf, veil”), but this is itself of unknown origin and the sense …

noun:Fähnlein.tx: From Fahne + -lein. Middle High German as venelîn, venel, venlîn, fänlîn, venlein, fendlî, vänl, vänel, venel, fendel. The secondary (metonymic) meaning dates to the first half of the 16th century.

noun:Fremdling.tx: From Middle High German vremdelinc, equivalent to fremd + -ling.

noun:Fisimatenten.tx: From Central Franconian visimetent (“nonsense”, attested 1499 in Cologne; now in the form Fissematente). Further origin unsettled. Possibly from Middle High German visament, fisiment (“ornamentation of a coat of arms”). Popular etymology has derived it from French je visite ma tante (“I'm visiting my aunt”), used as an excuse, or visitez ma tente (“visit my tent”), supposedly used by soldiers to …

noun:Freikorps.tx: Compound of frei + Korps, literally “free corps”.

noun:Fäule.tx: From Middle High German fūle, vūle, fiule, viule, from Old High German fūlī, from Proto-Germanic *fūlį̄, derivative of *fūlaz. Equivalent to faul + -e.

noun:Flex.tx: The device was first invented in 1954 and sold under the brand name Flex, which eventually entered common usage to refer to any such device. Apparently a clipping of flexibel.

verb:fremdgehen.tx: From fremd + gehen, thus “to go strange”, that is “to go with an outsider”.

phrase:frohes Schaffen.tx: Literally, “merry working!”, or more loosely translated as “energetic working!”.

noun:Fant.tx: Borrowed from Italian fante (“lad, chum”). Doublet of Infant.

noun:Fatwa.tx: Borrowed from Arabic فَتْوَى (fatwā, “formal legal opinion”), the verbal noun of أَفْتَى (ʔaftā, “to deliver a formal opinion”).

adj:famos.tx: From Latin famosus, partly through French fameux (“famed, renowned”).

adj:fesch.tx: Clipping of earlier fashionabel, from English fashionable.

adj:fetzig.tx: From the verb fetzen (“to carry away, inspire”)

adj:fluffig.tx: Late 20th century, from English fluffy. Along with Mulch one of the few recent borrowings that still received a spelling pronunciation.

adj:flügellahm.tx: From Flügel + lahm. Compare Dutch vleugellam.

adj:frevelhaft.tx: From Middle High German vrevelhaft. By surface analysis, Frevel + -haft.

adj:freventlich.tx: Derived from Middle High German vrevenlich by insertion of a -t- in the 16th century, from Middle High German vrevellich. Related to Old High German fravallīhho. Related to Frevel.

noun:Fourier.tx: Borrowed from French fourrier, derived from Old French fuerre (“hay; fodder”), from Frankish *fodar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder”), whence Futter. Doublet of Furier.

verb:funken.tx: From Middle High German vunken, equivalent to Funke + -en.

noun:Fratze.tx: Shortened from Fratzengesicht (“joker face”), from fratzen (“silly talk, jokes”), probably borrowed from Italian frasche (“nonsense”), plural of frasca (“vanity, caprice”). Cognate with Dutch fratsen.

noun:Fastfood.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English fast food.

noun:Feldstein.tx: From Middle High German veltstein. By surface analysis, Feld (“field”) + Stein (“stone”).

noun:Fehl.tx: From Middle High German væle, Old French faille (“failure”).

verb:frotzeln.tx: Uncertain, perhaps dialectal (Bavarian), related to Fratze (“sneer, grimace”), or from Italian frottola (“fib”).

noun:Fachidiot.tx: Functionally Fach + Idiot, perhaps from Fachidiotismus (1885), in common use since the late 1960s.

noun:Flansch.tx: According to Kluge, Pfeifer and Duden, from Middle High German vlansch (“corner, end”), with possible relations to Flunsch (“pout, pouty mouth”) and to flennen (“to cry noisily, snivel”). However, the likely descendant of the inherited term seems to show very little usage in New High German, and with the sense having shifted towartds "torn bit, strip of meat". The modern meaning of "flange" …

noun:Fäulnis.tx: From Middle High German fūlnis, vūlnis, fūlnisse, vūlnisse, from Old High German fūlnussī, from Proto-West Germanic *fūlnassī. Equivalent to Faul + -nis. Compare English foulness and Dutch vuilnis (“rubbish; garbage; trash”).

verb:fletschen.tx: From Middle High German vletschen (“bare one's teeth”), from or related to vletzen (“flatten, spread out”) (for the change of -tz- to -tsch, compare rutschen), related to Old High German flaȥ and English flat.

noun:Fasel.tx: From Middle High German vasel (“breeding animal”), from Old High German fasal (“offspring”), from Proto-Germanic *fas(u)laz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *pes- (“penis”).

noun:Fettnäpfchen.tx: From Fettnapf + -chen. The figurative sense is a backformation from the phrase ins Fettnäpfchen treten, which see.

verb:fehlleiten.tx: fehl + leiten. (Cognate equivalent would be fail-lead).

noun:Feldscher.tx: Clipping of Feldscherer, from Feld (“field”) + scheren (“shear, clip, crop”) + -er.

noun:Flottille.tx: Borrowed from French flottille, from Spanish flotilla.

verb:feixen.tx: From Feix (“young student”) + -en, maybe an altered form of Feist, dialect form of Fist (“soft fart”).

noun:Freiheitsberaubung.tx: From Freiheit (“freedom”) + -s- + Beraubung (“bereavement, deprivation”). Compare Dutch vrijheidsberoving, Swedish frihetsberövande.

noun:Feh.tx: From Middle High German vēch (“spotted, mottled fur”), from the adjective vēch, vēhe, vē (“multicoloured”, whence obsolete German fech, feh), from Old High German fēh, from Proto-West Germanic *faih, from Proto-Germanic *faihaz. Cognate with Scots faw.

noun:Fusel.tx: Borrowed from Low German Fusel, perhaps originally from Rotwelsch. Cognate with English fuzzle (“to make drunk, intoxicate”).

verb:frönen.tx: Middle High German vrœnen, Old High German frōnen, related to Fron (“socage”).

noun:Flachpfeife.tx: From flach (“flat”) + Pfeife (“pipe, whistle”). Pfeife already means “idiot” on its own. The extended form is comparable to Flachzange, another synonym.

verb:frachten.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German vrachten (compare Middle Dutch vrachten). By surface analysis, Fracht + -en.

verb:fächeln.tx: Iterative of fachen (-eln), probably with the later influence of Fächer. Since the 16th century.

verb:fingern.tx: From Middle High German vingern. By surface analysis, Finger + -en.

noun:Fußstapfen.tx: From Middle High German vuozstapfe, from Old High German fuozstapho.

noun:Frevler.tx: From Middle High German vrevelere, vrevelære, equivalent to Frevel + -er. Compare Middle Low German vrēvelære.

noun:Fittich.tx: From Middle High German vetech, vettech, from Old High German feddah, fettah, perhaps contracted from fedrah, fedarah, though this is uncertain. Either way probably related with Feder (“feather”).

noun:Froschfresser.tx: From Frosch (“frog”) + Fresser (“eater”). The derogatory use probably after English frogeater. Attestations from the 19th century are often in English contexts.

noun:Fliegenfänger.tx: From Fliege (“fly”) + -n- + Fänger (“catcher, one who catches”). The sports sense from the notion of someone trying to catch flies with their bare hands.

noun:Flöz.tx: From older flez, from Middle High German vletz, vletze (“threshing floor”), from Old High German flezzi, from Proto-West Germanic *flati, from Proto-Germanic *flatją (“floor”). Cognate with Low German Flett, Old English flett, Old Norse flet.

noun:Fürbitte.tx: From Middle High German vürbitte, vürbete.

noun:Fallsucht.tx: From fallen (“to fall”) + Sucht (here in the old sense “illness, disease”), thus the same as English falling sickness, Dutch vallende ziekte or Swedish fallandesot. Compare also Arabic صَرْع (ṣarʕ), Estonian langetõbi, Polish padaczka, Czech padoucnice, Russian паду́чая (padúčaja) Serbo-Croatian pȁdavica, all equally derived from a word for “to fall”. From the fits which cast the patients to the ground.

noun:Fußschemel.tx: From Proto-West Germanic *fōtskamil. Equivalent to Fuß (“foot”) + Schemel (“stool”).

noun:Frühgeborenes.tx: Nominalization of the adjective frühgeboren (“prematurely born, premature”, literally “early born”).

verb:fronen.tx: From Middle High German vrōnen, from Old High German frōnen.

verb:fortnehmen.tx: From fort- + nehmen. Compare Middle High German vürdernemen, fürdernemen.

verb:flimmern.tx: From an East Central German iterative construction flimmen + -ern, since the 17th century. flimmen is attested since the 16th century and is an ablauted variant of Middle High German vlammen, whence also German flammen.

adj:fingerbreit.tx: * Zero derivation of Fingerbreit, itself a compound of Finger (“finger”) + breit (“broad, wide”)

adj:faustdick.tx: A compound of Faust (“fist”) + dick (“big, fat, thick”), the adjective is documented since the 18th century, first as a unit of measurement, later oftentimes figuratively. In the second and third sense Faust is a symbol of rudeness and significance.

phrase:Fisch muss schwimmen.tx: Literally, “fish must swim”. Compare the same in Dutch vis moet zwemmen.

noun:Frauenhaus.tx: From Middle High German frouwenhūs, frōwenhūs, vrouwenhūs, vrounhūs, equivalent to Frau + -en- + Haus. Compare Middle Low German vrouwenhûs, Middle Dutch vrouwenhuus.

noun:Fallstudie.tx: From Fall + Studie. Calque of English case study.

noun:Freikörperkultur.tx: frei(er) + Körper + Kultur, literally “bare body culture”, euphemistically for earlier Nacktkultur (literally “nude culture”), 1920s.

noun:Funzel.tx: Unknown; maybe from funken + -sel (which properly would give *Funksel)

noun:Fehlleistung.tx: From fehl- + Leistung. Coined by Sigmund Freud.

verb:frankieren.tx: Borrow from Italian francare in the 17th century, derived from Italian (porto di) franco; see Italian franco (“frank, free”) for more.

noun:Fetisch.tx: Borrowed from French fétiche, from Portuguese feitiço, from Latin factīcius (“artificial”).

verb:faseln.tx: Uncertain, perhaps related to Norwegian and Swedish fjas (“chatter”).

verb:fachsimpeln.tx: From Fach (“discipline, field of expertise”) + simpeln (“to be stupid, talk nonsense”). Alternatively from Fachsimpel + -en, from Simpel (“simpleton”).

noun:Fist.tx: From Middle High German vist, from Proto-Germanic *fistiz, from Proto-Indo-European *pesd-. Cognate with Dutch veest and Ancient Greek πέζις (pézis, “puffball”).

noun:Firlefanz.tx: Perhaps from Middle High German firlifanz, a type of dance, or related to Alfanzerei.

verb:fußen.tx: From Middle High German vuoȥen. Compare Luxembourgish foussen.

noun:Flugmodus.tx: Flug + Modus, calque of English flight mode

verb:fächern.tx: From Fach (to divide). From Fächer (to fan).

verb:fläzen.tx: From Fläz (“lazybones”) + -en in the 2nd half of the 19th century, from Low German Fläz of unknown origin. Perhaps through Münster region vläts (“a loathsome person”) from Proto-West Germanic *wlātiþō or derived from the name of the theologian Matthias Flacius. Küpper instead connects the verb to Middle High German vletzen (“to spread out, spread flat”), but a seeming lack of written attestations …

phrase:früher war mehr Lametta.tx: Literally, “there used to be more tinsel [at Christmas]”, a catchphrase from the sketch Weihnachten bei Hoppenstedts (1978) by Loriot; itself probably a pun on the synonymous früher war alles besser.

noun:Fatzke.tx: Probably borrowed from Polish Wacku, the vocative form of Wacek, which is the diminutive form of the given name Wacław, itself from Czech Václav, from Old Czech Venceslav, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslàvъ. Doublet of Wenzel.

noun:Futteral.tx: 15th century, from Futter (“lining”, formerly also “sheath”) + -al. Said to have been formed after Medieval Latin fotrale, but this is sparsely attested and no earlier than the German; thus perhaps inspired by Middle French fourrel, from Old French forrel (11th c.). All words ultimately derive from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath, lining”).

noun:Freudenmädchen.tx: From Freude (“joy”) + -n- + Mädchen (“girl; maiden”). A calque of French fille de joie (“joy girl”). Cognate to English daughter of joy.

noun:Feiger.tx: From the obsolete Middle High German veic (“fated to die”), which evolved into the meaning of "easily intimidated, fearful, cowardly".

noun:Fitzel.tx: Diminutive of Fitze (“strand of yarn”). See also Fetzen (“scrap, rag”) and zerfetzen (“to tear apart, to lacerate, to shred”).

noun:Freite.tx: From Middle High German vrīete, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frijōną.

noun:Faszie.tx: Borrowed from Latin fascia (“a band, bandage, swathe”).

noun:Fickschlampe.tx: Calque of English fuckslut. By surface analysis, Fick (“fuck”) + Schlampe (“slut”).

noun:Faxenmacher.tx: From Faxe + -n- + Macher. Cognate with German Low German Faxenmaker (“clown, buffoon”).

noun:Forschender.tx: From forschend, present participle of forschen, following Studierender in usage.

noun:Fäkalie.tx: 19th c. Pseudo-Latinism, possibly from French fécal + Latin -ālie, from Middle French fecal, from Latin faex.

noun:Formans.tx: Coined by German linguist Karl Brugmann in 1904 from Latin elementum fōrmāns (“forming element”), with fōrmāns being the present participle of fōrmō (“to shape; to form; to fashion”). By surface analysis, formen + -ans. Doublet of Formant.

noun:Flummi.tx: Blend of fliegender (“flying”) + Gummi (“rubber”), after English flubber, which see. Note the different senses; flubber is called Schleim or Glibber in German. The use specifically for a ball through shortening of Flummiball.

noun:Fachärztin.tx: From Fach (“subject”) + Ärztin (“physician”) or rather Facharzt + -in with umlaut

verb:fortgeben.tx: fort- + geben. Cognate with Dutch voortgeven and English give forth.

noun:Freigelassener.tx: From freigelassen (“released”) + -er; a substantivization of freigelassen, past participle of freilassen.

noun:Flappe.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German flabbe. Cognate to English flap, Dutch flap.

verb:fleddern.tx: Said to be from thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch) fladdern (“to wash”). On the face of it, identity with etymology 2 below might also be considerable.

noun:Fuzzi.tx: From the fictional character “Fuzzy Q. Jones”, a bumbling cowboy and comical sidekick, a role played by Al St. John across many movies in the 1930s and 1940s. The character was named after actor John Forrest “Fuzzy” Knight (who played similar roles), from English fuzzy, a nickname given for his soft voice. Unusually, the pronunciation itself is not borrowed and instead re-derived by spelling …

adv:frühs.tx: From früh (“early”) + -s (adverbial genitive), possibly continuing Frühs, genitive of obsolete Früh n.

noun:Fettauge.tx: From Fett (“fat”) + Auge (“eye”). Compare Dutch vetoog and further French œil, Polish oczko etc.

noun:Fehlbezeichnung.tx: From fehl- (“mis-”) + Bezeichnung (“designation, denomination, name, term”).

noun:Filmkunst.tx: From Film + Kunst. Compare Danish filmkunst, Swedish filmkonst.

noun:Fliegengewicht.tx: Calque of English flyweight. By surface analysis, Fliege + -n- + Gewicht.

noun:Federgewicht.tx: Calque of English featherweight. By surface analysis, Feder + Gewicht.

noun:Fluchtverhalten.tx: From Flucht (“flight, the act of fleeing”) + Verhalten (“behavior”).

noun:Funktor.tx: From Funktion + -or, influenced by Faktor. Coined by German philosopher and logician Rudolf Carnap in 1934.

adj:fährlich.tx: From Middle High German værlich, from Old High German fāhrlīh, from Old High German fāra.

noun:Future.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from future. The masculine gender is likely inherited from Futures-Kontrakt.

noun:Fertilität.tx: From Latin fertilitas. By surface analysis, fertil + -ität.

noun:Fluidum.tx: From Latin fluidum, neuter singular of fluidus.

noun:Fräse.tx: 19th century, from French fraise, from Old French fraise (“tripe”), ultimately from Latin frēsus, past participle of frendere (“to grind”). The French word first developed the sense “ruff, frill” by analogy with the appearance of tripe, and thence later the sense “milling cutter” by another analogy of appearance.
